item.title: BoE preview: MUFG expects November rate hike as energy shock pushes UK inflation above 4%
item.description:
A hike on November 5 would extend the energy-driven tightening seen across central banks. Any guidance pointing to a February follow-up would likely support sterling, particularly against currencies where central banks are seen as slower to respond. Gilts look the more vulnerable asset: 10-year UK yields already sit at the top of the G7 range, and further tightening alongside reduced fiscal headroom ahead of the Budget could keep pressure on longer-dated debt. For equities, higher rates and energy costs weigh on domestically focused UK stocks, while the FTSE 100’s energy-heavy constituents offer some offset. Oil and gas remain the key swing factor: with household energy bills driving the expected rise in inflation, any further spike in prices linked to the Middle East war would strengthen the case for a longer hiking cycle.

---

Earlier:

  • UK September CPI inflation rises to 3.5%, reinforces BOE November rate hike expectations

---

MUFG says the Bank of England cannot look through this energy shock the way it might like, because the UK economy is simply too strong to make waiting look safe.

Summary:

  • MUFG expects the Bank of England to raise rates by 25 basis points at its next meeting, with another hike in February to a 4.25% peak
  • UK headline inflation is seen rising above 4% in coming months as higher energy prices feed through to household bills
  • Energy prices have stayed elevated for longer than expected and have risen further in recent months, MUFG says
  • A stabilising labour market, healthy growth and elevated underlying inflation leave the Bank of England struggling to look through the shock
  • MUFG says UK Q3 GDP is tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter, and it forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, above IMF projections
  • Higher borrowing costs may have cut fiscal headroom to around £15 billion ahead of the Budget

The Bank of England is likely to raise interest rates at its next meeting, as higher energy prices push UK inflation back above 4%, according to MUFG, which expects a further increase in February.

In its European macro and market outlook, MUFG said it expects a 25 basis point hike at the Bank of England’s next policy decision, due on November 5, followed by another in February, taking Bank Rate to a terminal level of 4.25%. The bank said energy prices have remained elevated for longer than anticipated and have moved higher in recent months. As those costs feed through to household bills, it expects headline inflation to rise above 4%.

MUFG argued that the Bank of England will struggle to look through the energy shock, as it might otherwise, because of the wider economic backdrop. The labour market is stabilising, growth is healthy and underlying inflation remains elevated. Services inflation measures are still running well above the Bank’s 2% target.

The UK economy has been notably resilient. MUFG said recent activity data have consistently surprised to the upside, and the economy does not appear to be repeating the second-half slowdowns of recent years, with third-quarter GDP tracking at about 0.65% quarter on quarter. It forecasts growth of 1.5% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027, more optimistic than the IMF, despite energy-related headwinds.

That growth is fairly narrow, however, led by professional services and other knowledge-intensive sectors. MUFG said it is too early to draw firm conclusions, but the UK’s comparatively rapid adoption of artificial intelligence could help explain recent productivity gains. The share of UK job postings mentioning AI has risen faster than in the US or major European economies.

The fiscal backdrop is a complicating factor. MUFG estimates that higher borrowing costs may have reduced the government’s headroom against its fiscal rules to around £15 billion. It expects the upcoming Budget to include some offsetting tax measures alongside temporary, targeted support for households facing higher energy bills. MUFG questioned whether reducing fiscal buffers is prudent while growth holds up and geopolitical uncertainty remains high.

The Bank of England’s decision is due at 12:00 GMT (07:00 US Eastern time) on November 5. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: New Zealand inflation slows to 3.7% in Q3, below forecasts, keeping RBNZ hike on track
item.description:
The miss was too small to shift the policy outlook. Markets still price an October 28 hike as near certain and a cumulative 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February. The kiwi’s dip just below 0.57 suggests traders trimmed only the most aggressive hike bets. Oil is the key swing factor from here: the Middle East war is lifting fuel, fertiliser and transport costs, and with petrol already the biggest contributor to inflation, any further rise in crude feeds directly into the expected fourth-quarter rebound. That keeps the risk skewed toward a longer tightening cycle. NZD support is likely to depend on how hawkish the RBNZ’s guidance proves next week rather than on today’s data.

-

Earlier:

  • New Zealand Q3 CPI 3.7% y/y (expected 3.8%, prior 4.1%)

-

New Zealand’s inflation undershot forecasts, but with core pressures firm and fuel prices climbing again, the miss looks more like a pause in the problem than a turn in it.

Summary:

  • Annual CPI slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter from 4.1%, below the 3.8% Reuters poll forecast and the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection
  • Quarterly CPI rose 0.7%, against expectations of 0.8%
  • Petrol was the largest contributor to inflation despite easing from the June quarter; house-building costs also rose
  • Non-tradeable inflation eased to 3.3% from 3.4%, while tradeable inflation was 4.3%
  • Markets price a 98% chance of a hike next week and a full 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February; the NZD dipped to around 0.569
  • Economists expect inflation to rebound in the fourth quarter, with ASB forecasting 4.5% by year-end

New Zealand’s annual inflation slowed to 3.7% in the third quarter, below economists’ forecasts but still above the top of the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s target range, official data showed on Thursday. The result did little to shift expectations that the central bank will raise interest rates next week.

The consumer price index rose 0.7% from the second quarter, Statistics New Zealand said, compared with a 0.8% increase expected by economists polled by Reuters. The annual rate eased from 4.1% in the June quarter and came in below both the 3.8% consensus and the RBNZ’s own 3.9% projection. The central bank targets annual inflation of 1% to 3% over the medium term.

Statistics New Zealand said petrol prices were the largest contributor to inflation, even though they had eased from the June quarter, and that house-building costs had also risen. Non-tradeable inflation, which captures domestically driven price pressures, eased to 3.3% from 3.4%. Tradeable inflation, which covers imported goods including fuel, was 4.3%.

The New Zealand dollar dipped to around 0.569 against the US dollar after the release. However, markets continue to price a 98% chance of a rate hike at next week’s monetary policy review, and fully price 50 basis points of tightening by the end of February. The RBNZ has raised the official cash rate twice this year to 2.75%.

Westpac New Zealand senior economist Satish Ranchhod said that although the result was below the RBNZ’s forecast, firm core inflation would give policymakers pause for thought. He said a hike next week now looked like the path of least resistance, with market pricing and economist views converging on a move.

Economists expect inflation to pick up again in the fourth quarter as fuel prices rise once more. ASB forecasts inflation of 4.5% by year-end and said its 2027 profile looks considerably firmer than the RBNZ’s September projections. The Middle East war is adding to stagflation risks globally by disrupting energy supplies and shipping, which is lifting fuel, fertiliser and transport costs.

The data is the last major release before the RBNZ’s decision. It lands as inflation becomes a central issue ahead of the closely contested November 7 general election.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Bank of Korea expected to hold rates today after two hikes, tightening cycle seen intact
item.description:
A hold is fully expected, so the market reaction is likely to hinge on the tone of the statement and any signal on the timing of the next hike. A hawkish hold that keeps a further increase firmly on the table would likely support the won and push short-dated Korean government bond yields higher. Any hint that the cycle is nearing its end could weigh on the currency. For equities, a pause offers some relief to rate-sensitive sectors. The semiconductor-led export boom underpinning growth keeps chipmakers at the centre of the market’s growth story. A record-scale current account surplus provides an underlying source of support for the won, even as policy expectations drive day-to-day moves.

-The Bank of Korea is expected to catch its breath today rather than call time on tightening, with booming chip exports and stubborn price pressures keeping the next hike in view.

Summary:

  • All six economists surveyed by Yonhap expect the Bank of Korea to leave its benchmark rate unchanged today
  • The Bank of Korea base rate is currently 3.00%
  • The central bank raised rates in July and August, and a third consecutive hike would be rare
  • Economists expect it to keep a tightening stance, pausing to adjust the pace of policy and assess the timing of further increases
  • Strong semiconductor exports are driving growth, while inflation pressures are coming from both supply and demand
  • The tightening cycle may continue in the short term, according to the survey
  • South Korea’s current account surplus for January to August reached about $279 billion, nearly four times the roughly $70 billion a year earlier
  • Announcment due at  GMT / 2100 US Eastern time 

-

The Bank of Korea is expected to leave interest rates unchanged at its policy meeting today, pausing after two consecutive hikes, though economists say its tightening cycle is not yet over.

All six economists surveyed by Yonhap News Agency expect the central bank to hold its benchmark rate, which stands at 3.00% following increases in July and August. Respondents said the Bank of Korea is likely to maintain its tight policy stance. However, they see a pause as more likely than a rare third straight hike, giving policymakers room to adjust the pace of tightening and judge when further increases might be needed.

The economists pointed to a backdrop that still argues for tighter policy. Strong semiconductor exports are driving economic growth, while inflation is facing upward pressure from both supply-side and demand-side factors. Taken together, those conditions suggest the hiking cycle could continue in the near term, according to the survey.

The strength of the export sector is reflected in South Korea’s external accounts. The cumulative current account surplus for January to August reached about $279 billion, nearly four times the roughly $70 billion recorded in the same period last year. The surplus highlights how heavily the economy is benefiting from global demand for memory chips and other semiconductor products, a key source of growth that has given the central bank room to tighten without derailing the expansion.

A hold would mark a shift in tempo rather than direction. Markets are likely to focus closely on the central bank’s statement and on any guidance about the timing of the next move, for signals on whether policymakers see a further hike as likely in the coming months. The balance between growth driven by strong exports and persistent price pressures will be central to that assessment, alongside the outlook for the won and domestic demand. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: BlackRock’s Hambro sees gold rising on debt and deficits
item.description:
Hambro’s view adds a heavyweight institutional voice to the fiscal-debasement case for gold. It suggests that dips driven by shifting rate expectations may be treated as buying opportunities rather than a change in trend. His argument that mining costs are rising more slowly than the gold price supports the case for further margin expansion and equity outperformance across the sector, including copper producers. The buyback criticism carries weight given BlackRock’s large stakes in Newmont, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields. It could push gold majors toward more flexible capital returns, or toward redirecting cash into new mine development. For bond markets, his warning that governments will need to pay higher interest to attract lenders points to continued upward pressure on longer-dated yields.

-

BlackRock’s Evy Hambro sees gold as insurance against governments that cannot stop borrowing, and he wants the gold miners to spend their windfall more wisely than those governments do.

Summary:

  • Evy Hambro, BlackRock’s global head of thematic and sector investing, expects gold to keep appreciating as government debt, deficits and currency depreciation worsen
  • He says government bond markets are signalling that public finances are unhealthy, and that inflating away debt may make central banks less strict about hitting inflation targets
  • He argues gold miners once again offer about three times leverage to the gold price, because mining costs are rising more slowly than prices
  • He sees gold as portfolio insurance and says allocations remain far smaller than the roughly 10% often suggested
  • He criticised Barrick Mining, Newmont, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields over about $12 billion in buybacks, saying they lacked proper process; BlackRock holds sizeable stakes in three of them
  • BlackRock expects near-term volatility from shifting rate expectations but sees gold’s long-term trend as higher

Gold is set to keep rising as government debt, budget deficits and currency depreciation worsen, according to Evy Hambro, global head of thematic and sector investing at BlackRock. He also said gold mining shares are once again delivering amplified returns relative to the metal.

In an interview with MoneyWeek, Hambro said he expects the current environment of mild stagflation, a weak dollar and geopolitical turmoil to persist. He argued that government bond markets are signalling that public finances are unhealthy, with rising yields reflecting very large debt levels and growing annual deficits. In his view, investors are increasingly reluctant to lend to governments that spend poorly and have no plan to tackle their debts, and will demand much higher interest rates to do so.

Hambro said real assets such as infrastructure, commodities and gold have historically protected purchasing power. He noted that when he began his career around three decades ago, copper traded near 60 cents a pound and gold around $400 an ounce, compared with roughly $6 and $4,000 now. He described gold as portfolio insurance. Wealth managers commonly held it in the 1990s, but allocations largely disappeared in the early 2000s, and he said they have returned at far smaller weightings than the roughly 10% often suggested.

He said the least painful way for governments to reduce debt is to inflate it away. That suggests central banks may be less strict about hitting inflation targets they already frequently miss.

On mining equities, Hambro said the historical relationship in which gold shares moved about three times as much as the gold price is fully intact again. That reflects mining costs rising more slowly than prices, which has expanded margins. He said physically backed gold ETFs suit investors who want pure price exposure, while mining shares offer more upside, along with dividends and growth.

Hambro was sharply critical of gold majors’ share buybacks, however. Speaking at the FT Mining Summit last week, he described recent programmes as reckless and said they had been approved without proper process. Barrick Mining, Newmont, AngloGold Ashanti and Gold Fields have announced buybacks worth around $12 billion, and BlackRock owns about 12% of Newmont, 10% of AngloGold Ashanti and 6% of Gold Fields. He said companies should keep the flexibility to buy back shares when prices are low, rather than committing to large programmes near the peak.

Hambro said BlackRock expects near-term volatility in gold as monetary policy and interest rate expectations shift, but sees the long-term trend remaining firmly higher.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: JPMorgan doubles SpaceX target to $500 on AI growth, maps out possible Tesla merger
item.description:
JPMorgan’s call reinforces the market’s shift toward valuing SpaceX as an AI infrastructure company rather than a launch and satellite business. That raises the stakes on its ability to build compute capacity and fund it. For Tesla shareholders, a 30% to 35% premium framework gives the merger speculation a concrete reference point and may help underpin the shares while the special committees do their work. China remains the main overhang, given Tesla’s exposure to the Chinese market and SpaceX’s defence ties. Any deal structure that ring-fences or spins off that business would carry its own valuation questions. The heavy capital needs JPMorgan flags also feed into the wider debate over AI-related financing, with SpaceX saying it is not considering an equity raise.

---

Yesterday:

  • SpaceX beats Q3 forecasts across all three segments as AI revenue tops $7.5 billion

--- JPMorgan now values SpaceX more as an AI powerhouse than a rocket company, and it has already sketched out what Tesla shareholders might be offered if Musk brings his two biggest companies together.

Summary:

  • JPMorgan raised its SpaceX price target to $500 from $240 and kept an Overweight rating after the company’s third-quarter results
  • The bank more than doubled its 2027 and 2028 estimates, naming superintelligence as the main growth driver
  • It forecasts 2027 revenue of about $254 billion, and bases its target on 20 times its 2028 earnings per share estimate of about $24
  • JPMorgan flagged execution risks around expanding compute capacity, raising capital and sustaining demand; SpaceX told the bank it is not considering an equity raise
  • It sees any Tesla merger as a likely SpaceX-led all-stock deal at a 30% to 35% premium to Tesla’s share price, with Musk keeping more than 50% voting control
  • China is the key regulatory hurdle, and JPMorgan kept its Neutral rating and $415 target on Tesla

JPMorgan has more than doubled its price target on SpaceX to $500 from $240, keeping an Overweight rating after the company’s third-quarter results. The bank argues that artificial intelligence, rather than its launch business, is now the main driver of the company’s growth.

Analyst Doug Anmuth said SpaceX beat sales expectations across all three of its business segments, and he identified superintelligence as the principal growth engine. JPMorgan more than doubled its 2027 and 2028 forecasts and now expects 2027 revenue of about $254 billion. It projects annual recurring revenue of about $400 billion by the end of 2027, below management’s own expected range of $500 billion to $1 trillion. The new target is based on 20 times JPMorgan’s 2028 earnings per share estimate of about $24.

The bank cautioned that reaching those estimates will require significant execution, including building out compute capacity, securing substantial capital and sustaining strong demand. SpaceX expects to have 2 to 3 gigawatts of compute capacity by the end of 2026 and plans to add 10 gigawatts in 2027. It told JPMorgan it is not considering raising equity.

The note also addresses a potential combination with Tesla, after Elon Musk said on SpaceX’s earnings call that both companies had formed special committees to discuss a merger. JPMorgan sees the most likely structure as a SpaceX-led, all-stock deal at a 30% to 35% premium to Tesla’s share price. It would be structured as a merger of equals that keeps Musk’s voting control above 50%. The bank described the strategic logic as coherent, pointing to shared engineering talent, AI infrastructure, the Terafab chip facility in Texas and Musk’s leadership.

Shareholder and regulatory approval are the key hurdles, according to JPMorgan, with China the particular challenge given SpaceX’s ties to the US government and defence sector. Possible solutions include ring-fencing Tesla’s China operations or transferring control of them to a China-based consortium. Under that arrangement, Tesla could continue to earn revenue by licensing its brand and Full Self-Driving technology.

JPMorgan kept its Neutral rating and $415 price target on Tesla. SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of about $14.6 billion, up 161% from a year earlier, with adjusted EBITDA up about 306% to around $8.8 billion, both ahead of consensus.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tesla earnings call: Targets 5 million cars a year by 2030, says 2027 Megapack supply nearly sold out
item.description:
The call recasts Tesla’s third-quarter energy shortfall as a supply constraint rather than a demand problem. That may limit the damage from the segment’s sizeable revenue miss, particularly with management guiding to meaningfully higher storage margins. On the balance sheet, more than $45 billion in cash and investments, capex funded mainly from operating cash flow and no plans to draw on new credit lines this year point to a comfortable funding position. That may ease worries about the cost of its autonomy and chip ambitions. The $30 billion facility nonetheless signals that heavier spending is likely in later years. Mark-to-market swings on SpaceX and Bitcoin holdings add a layer of noise to reported earnings. Combined with Musk’s refusal to add to his SpaceX merger comments, they keep the link between the two companies in focus.

---

Earlier:

  • Tesla Q3 earnings beat as margins and cash flow surprise, revenue narrowly misses

---

Tesla’s energy business missed on revenue but not, management insists, on demand, as Musk paired a sold-out Megapack order book with fresh volume, robotaxi and chip ambitions, backed by a balance sheet with plenty in reserve.

Summary:

  • Tesla is targeting production of about 5 million vehicles a year by 2030 and plans to raise output to meet demand, CEO Elon Musk said on the earnings call
  • Nearly all 2027 Megapack capacity is sold out. Management expects energy storage margins to rise meaningfully and significant growth after several relatively flat years
  • The Cybercab fleet in Austin has grown about tenfold since launching roughly a month ago, with autonomous miles growing rapidly week on week
  • First test chips are targeted for May to June 2027, subject to machinery commissioning that is due to begin in the first half of the year
  • Full-year capex guidance has been revised to about $20 billion, funded mainly by operating cash flow
  • Tesla has secured up to $30 billion in additional borrowing capacity, with no drawdowns planned in 2026; cash and investments exceed $45 billion
  • A mark-to-market loss of about $140 million on its SpaceX investment hit net income, offset by a gain of about $290 million on Bitcoin
  • Musk declined to add to his SpaceX merger comments, saying he had covered the topic on the SpaceX call a day earlier

Tesla is aiming to produce about 5 million vehicles a year by 2030 and will increase production to meet demand, Chief Executive Elon Musk said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call. Management also said demand for its energy storage products remains very strong, despite a sizeable revenue miss in that business.

Nearly all of Tesla’s 2027 capacity for Megapack, its large-scale battery storage system for utilities and grid operators, is already sold out, according to management. Production is being ramped as quickly as possible to meet demand. Tesla expects energy storage gross margins to increase meaningfully, and significant growth after several years of relatively flat performance. The comments suggest that the third-quarter shortfall in energy generation and storage revenue, which came in at about $2.9 billion against estimates near $3.9 billion, reflected supply constraints rather than weakening demand.

Tesla also highlighted progress in autonomous driving. Fully autonomous miles driven are growing exponentially, with rapid week-on-week acceleration, and the Cybercab fleet in Austin has expanded roughly tenfold since launching about a month ago. Management pointed to substantial potential to scale robotaxi operations, although it did not give absolute fleet or mileage figures.

On chip manufacturing, Tesla said machinery commissioning is scheduled to begin in the first half of 2027. First test chip production is targeted for May to June 2027, subject to successful commissioning, with an initial focus on demonstrating basic manufacturing capability.

On the financial side, Tesla revised its full-year capital expenditure guidance to about $20 billion, which it said reflects more efficient capital deployment. It expects to fund capex primarily from operating cash flow. The company has also secured up to $30 billion in additional borrowing capacity to support future capex growth, but does not plan to draw on the new facilities in 2026. Tesla ended the quarter with more than $45 billion in cash and investments, and free cash flow of over $1.5 billion.

Net income was affected by a mark-to-market loss of about $140 million on Tesla’s investment in SpaceX. A gain of about $290 million on its Bitcoin holdings offset that loss. Asked about a potential merger with SpaceX, Musk declined to elaborate, saying he had already said everything he needed to on the SpaceX call held the previous day.

The call follows third-quarter results in which adjusted earnings, gross margin and free cash flow beat expectations, while revenue narrowly missed. The energy ramp, robotaxi scale-up and the pace of future spending are likely to be key focus points as investors assess whether Tesla can turn these ambitions into sustained growth.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: More on Meta earnings (call): Plans effective 2-for-1 split via non-voting shares, confirms $9.9B Q3 legal charge
item.description:
Confirmation that the $9.9 billion charge was booked in the third quarter reframes the operating income miss as largely one-off. That should ease concerns that rising core costs drove the shortfall. The effective stock split, delivered through non-voting shares, lowers the per-share price without diluting existing holders’ voting power. That means it is likely to be welcomed by retail investors while drawing governance scrutiny from institutions. Upcoming US youth-related trials remain a legal overhang that could bring further charges, keeping litigation risk in focus beyond this quarter. The roughly 1% currency headwind built into Q4 guidance is modest, but it suggests the revenue outlook carries little help from a weaker dollar.

---

Earlier:

  • Meta Q3 beats on revenue and EPS as $9.9B legal charge lifts full-year expense outlook

---

Meta’s earnings call turned a messy profit miss into a cleaner story, pinning the shortfall on a one-off legal charge while unveiling a share split that leaves Mark Zuckerberg’s control untouched.

Summary:

  • Meta plans an effective 2-for-1 stock split by issuing one new non-voting share for each existing share, with trading expected to begin in late January 2027
  • The company confirmed the $9.9 billion legal charge was booked in the third quarter and is included in its raised full-year expense guidance of $175 billion to $179 billion
  • Excluding the charge, full-year operating income is expected to exceed 2025 levels
  • Reality Labs is expected to lose $18 billion to $19 billion this year, a smaller loss than last year
  • Q4 revenue guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion assumes a currency headwind of about 1%; the Q4 tax rate is guided at 15% to 17%
  • Capex guidance of $135 billion to $145 billion includes finance lease principal payments
  • Meta flagged ongoing legal and regulatory scrutiny, including upcoming US youth-related trials

Meta Platforms plans an effective 2-for-1 stock split through the issuance of a new class of non-voting shares, the company said on its third-quarter earnings call. It also confirmed that a $9.9 billion legal charge was booked in the quarter, largely accounting for the operating income shortfall in its results.

Under the plan, shareholders will receive one new non-voting share for each existing share they hold, with the new shares expected to begin trading in late January 2027. Structuring the split through non-voting stock doubles the share count without changing the balance of voting control. Meta had flagged the creation of the new Class C common stock in its results release, and the call clarified its purpose.

Meta said its full-year expense guidance of $175 billion to $179 billion, raised from $165 billion to $169 billion, includes the third-quarter legal charge. Excluding that charge, the company expects full-year operating income to exceed 2025 levels. Third-quarter operating income came in at about $13 billion, well below analyst estimates of roughly $20.9 billion.

The company also flagged ongoing legal and regulatory scrutiny, including upcoming US trials related to young users, an area that could keep litigation risk in focus.

For the fourth quarter, Meta reiterated revenue guidance of $73 billion to $76 billion, compared with consensus of around $73.6 billion. That outlook assumes a currency headwind of about 1% year on year. It expects a fourth-quarter effective tax rate of 15% to 17%.

Capital expenditure guidance was narrowed to $135 billion to $145 billion from $130 billion to $145 billion. Meta said the range includes principal payments on finance leases. In its Reality Labs division, the company expects a full-year loss of $18 billion to $19 billion, which it said would be lower than last year.

Meta pointed to strong execution in the quarter across its core advertising and engagement initiatives. It said it continues to make progress on its personal superintelligence strategy, its long-term push to build advanced AI assistants for individual users.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Reports: US reduces troops and diplomats across Middle East amid threat of military action on Iran
item.description:
Oil is the clearest channel for this news. Drawdowns of troops and diplomats are typically read as a signal that the risk of military action is rising, and that is likely to add to the geopolitical risk premium in crude, particularly given the Gulf’s central role in global supply. Traders are likely to watch for any threat to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz or to Saudi energy infrastructure, where disruption would hit physical supply rather than just sentiment. Haven assets such as gold, the US dollar and Treasuries could see support if the moves are followed by confirmation of military action. Risk-sensitive currencies and equities in energy-importing Asian economies may come under pressure. Confirmation from the Pentagon or State Department on the scale of the drawdown would help markets judge whether this is a precaution or a precursor.

-

Washington is thinning out its people across the Middle East, and when the US clears its posts ahead of a possible strike on Iran, oil markets tend to take notice.

Summary:

  • NBC News, citing two US officials, reports that the US military is reducing troop presence at bases across the Middle East
  • The State Department is ordering further staff reductions at diplomatic posts in the region, according to the report
  • The moves come amid regional threats and potential US military action against Iran
  • Hours earlier, the State Department ordered the departure of non-emergency government employees and their families from Saudi Arabia
  • Reuters had earlier reported that the State Department was preparing ordered departures at embassies across the Gulf, though the formal order initially covered Saudi Arabia only

The US military is reducing its troop presence at bases across the Middle East, while the State Department is ordering further staff cuts at diplomatic posts in the region, NBC News reported, citing two US officials. The report links the moves to regional threats and the possibility of US military action against Iran.

The NBC report followed a State Department order, issued a few hours earlier, for non-emergency US government employees and their family members to leave Saudi Arabia. An ordered departure is a formal instruction, rather than a voluntary option, and is typically used when the department judges that security conditions have deteriorated enough to justify reducing staff.

Earlier, Reuters had reported that the State Department was preparing ordered departures for some personnel and family members at US embassies across the Gulf. However, the formal order initially applied to Saudi Arabia only. The NBC report now points to a broader pullback covering both military and diplomatic personnel across the region, although the specific bases, posts and numbers involved were not detailed.

The scale and timing of the moves will be watched closely for signals about Washington’s intentions. Reducing the number of personnel exposed to potential retaliation is a standard precaution when the risk of conflict rises. That means the drawdown does not by itself confirm that military action is imminent or has been decided. Neither the Pentagon nor the State Department had publicly detailed the wider reductions at the time of the report.

The developments come as tensions over Iran remain at the centre of energy market concerns, with the Gulf region accounting for a large share of global oil exports and much of that supply passing through the Strait of Hormuz. Markets are likely to focus on any official confirmation of the drawdown, any statements from Tehran, and any further changes to the US posture at embassies and bases elsewhere in the Gulf.

item.title: BlackRock’s Rieder sees historic opportunity in high-grade bonds, including hyperscalers
item.description:
Rieder’s call adds a heavyweight voice to the argument that higher yields are now drawing large investors back into fixed income. That could help absorb the wave of AI-related corporate issuance that has weighed on credit markets. Support from the world’s largest asset manager may help stabilise spreads on hyperscaler bonds in particular, while debt tied to data centres without hyperscaler backing looks set to stay under pressure. For Treasuries, his warning that rates could still rise, along with his concern over government debt costs and crowding out from AI supply, suggests the bond buying case rests on income rather than price gains. With markets pricing a December Fed hike at close to 90%, the main near-term risk to the trade remains an inflation upside surprise. Higher oil prices remain a key driver of that risk.

-

BlackRock’s bond chief says investors are being paid crisis-level yields without a crisis, and the hyperscalers flooding the market with debt are among the borrowers he most wants to lend to.

Summary:

  • Rick Rieder, BlackRock’s chief investment officer for global fixed income, sees a historic opportunity in high-quality bonds, he told CNBC
  • He says investors could build a diversified portfolio yielding above 7%, with under three years of duration and an average A- credit rating
  • Investment-grade corporates are his top pick, including bonds from AI hyperscalers such as Alphabet, Amazon, Meta and Oracle, which have issued around $228 billion in debt this year
  • His iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has lifted its investment-grade allocation to about 14% from 8.5% in July
  • He remains cautious on data centre debt without hyperscaler backing and on lower-rated credit more broadly
  • He expects the Fed to hike in December but disagrees with the move, arguing that higher rates hurt housing and consumer credit while barely touching AI spending

BlackRock’s Rick Rieder says investors have a historic opportunity to secure attractive yields in high-quality bonds, despite volatility in parts of the credit market. He named investment-grade corporate debt as his preferred area for the first time in a long while.

Speaking to CNBC about his fourth-quarter outlook, Rieder, chief investment officer for global fixed income at the world’s largest asset manager, said investors could in theory build a diversified portfolio yielding more than 7%, with less than three years of duration and an average credit rating of A-. Duration measures a bond’s sensitivity to interest rate changes, so a shorter duration means less price risk if yields rise.

Rieder argued that yields at these levels usually appear only during an economic or default crisis. That is not the case now, he said, because the economy remains strong and he does not expect significant defaults.

Among his top opportunities are bonds issued by the hyperscalers, the large technology companies building AI infrastructure. Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms and Oracle have together issued around $228 billion in bonds this year as of October 20, according to LSEG data. Rieder said these companies carry low leverage and strong cash flow, meaning investors are being paid an attractive yield to lend to high-quality borrowers. His iShares Flexible Income Active ETF has raised its investment-grade corporate allocation to about 14%, from 8.5% in July.

He urged patience, warning that rates could still move higher. He argued that the starting yield is the best guide to returns for investors holding for a year or more. He also stressed caution outside investment grade, including parts of data centre financing that lack hyperscaler guarantees or backing.

The comments follow BlackRock’s move last week to upgrade short-dated US Treasuries to overweight, on the view that markets had overpriced Federal Reserve tightening. Rieder’s enthusiasm for investment-grade credit stands in contrast to the BlackRock Investment Institute’s recent research, which had steered away from the asset class because of heavy AI-related issuance.

On policy, Rieder expects the Fed to raise rates in December, with markets pricing that outcome at close to 90% according to the CME FedWatch tool. However, he does not agree with the move. He said higher rates are hurting rate-sensitive areas such as housing, credit cards and auto loans, while doing little to slow tech capital spending, which is not funded off the overnight rate.

Rieder also flagged risks from rising government debt globally, noting that the US budget deficit has grown to $2 trillion for fiscal 2026. He warned that higher rates add to borrowing costs for already indebted governments, and that heavy AI bond supply is beginning to crowd out other borrowers as government yields rise. 

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: Tesla Q3 earnings beat as margins and cash flow surprise, revenue narrowly misses
item.description:
The quarter is likely to be read as a profitability and cash story rather than a growth story. A margin beat of nearly two percentage points and positive free cash flow ease concerns about pricing pressure and spending. The sharp miss in energy generation and storage is the notable soft spot, given that the segment has been one of the bull case’s diversification arguments, so investors are likely to want an explanation of whether it reflects timing or demand. FSD subscriptions running ahead of expectations support the narrative of growing recurring software revenue. Without guidance in the headline figures, the reaction may lean heavily on management commentary on volumes, autonomy and capital spending.

Earlier (yesterday):

  • SpaceX’s Musk says Tesla merger good idea but far from certain, needs 50% of Tesla shares

-

Tesla delivered stronger margins and an unexpected cash inflow in the third quarter, but a steep shortfall in its energy business kept revenue just short of forecasts.

Summary:

  • Adjusted EPS of $0.48 beat the $0.44 estimate; GAAP EPS fell to $0.22 from $0.39 a year earlier
  • Revenue of about $28.05 billion came in just below the roughly $28.13 billion forecast
  • Gross margin of 19.6% topped expectations of 17.8%
  • Automotive revenue of about $20.6 billion and services and other revenue of about $4.6 billion both beat estimates
  • Energy generation and storage revenue of about $2.9 billion fell well short of the roughly $3.9 billion expected
  • Operating income of about $720 million beat the roughly $600 million estimate
  • Free cash flow of about $1.5 billion compared with a forecast outflow of around $5 billion
  • Active FSD subscriptions reached about 1.74 million, ahead of the 1.57 million expected; trailing 12-month revenue stayed above $100 billion for a second straight quarter

Tesla reported third-quarter 2026 adjusted earnings ahead of analyst expectations, supported by a stronger-than-forecast gross margin and a surprise positive free cash flow result. Total revenue came in marginally below estimates, as weakness in the company’s energy business offset gains in automotive and services.

Adjusted earnings per share were $0.48, compared with consensus estimates of $0.44. On a GAAP basis, earnings per share fell to $0.22 from $0.39 in the same quarter a year earlier. Revenue was about $28.05 billion, slightly below the roughly $28.13 billion analysts had expected.

Gross margin was a highlight at 19.6%, well above the 17.8% forecast. Operating income of about $720 million also exceeded expectations of around $600 million.

Automotive revenue reached about $20.6 billion, ahead of estimates near $19.8 billion. Services and other revenue came in at about $4.6 billion against forecasts of around $4.3 billion. The weak spot was energy generation and storage, where revenue of about $2.9 billion fell well short of the roughly $3.9 billion analysts had pencilled in.

Free cash flow was perhaps the most striking figure. Tesla generated about $1.5 billion in the quarter, while analysts had expected an outflow of around $5 billion.

The company’s self-driving software also showed momentum. Active Full Self-Driving (FSD) subscriptions reached about 1.74 million, ahead of the 1.57 million expected. FSD is Tesla’s paid driver-assistance software package, and subscription numbers are watched as a gauge of its recurring software revenue potential. Tesla also said trailing 12-month revenue remained above $100 billion for a second consecutive quarter.

The results leave a mixed picture for investors. Margins, cash generation and software uptake outperformed. However, the energy segment’s sizeable miss and the year-on-year fall in GAAP earnings are likely to draw scrutiny. Attention is likely to turn to management commentary on the energy business, vehicle demand and capital spending plans for clues on whether the quarter’s profitability gains can be sustained.

Meta Platforms reported third-quarter 2026 earnings and revenue ahead of analyst expectations, driven by continued strength in advertising. However, operating income fell well short of forecasts, and the company raised its full-year expense outlook to incorporate a legal charge of about $9.9 billion.

Earnings per share came in at $3.83, compared with consensus estimates of $3.57. Total revenue rose to about $64.6 billion, beating expectations of roughly $63.3 billion. Advertising revenue, which accounts for the overwhelming majority of the company’s sales, reached about $63.1 billion against forecasts near $61.9 billion. Revenue from the Family of Apps segment, which houses Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, came in at about $64.2 billion, ahead of the roughly $62.8 billion expected.

Profitability told a different story. Operating income of about $13 billion was well below the roughly $20.9 billion analysts had forecast, and Family of Apps operating income of about $17.1 billion missed estimates of around $23.3 billion.

In the Reality Labs division, which develops virtual and augmented reality hardware, revenue of about $440 million fell short of the roughly $518 million expected. The unit’s operating loss of about $4.1 billion was narrower than the forecast loss of around $5.1 billion.

Meta said it now expects full-year total expenses of $175 billion to $179 billion, up from its previous range of $165 billion to $169 billion. The company said the higher outlook incorporates the $9.9 billion legal charge, which broadly accounts for the $10 billion lift at both ends of the range. Capital expenditure guidance was narrowed to $135 billion to $145 billion from $130 billion to $145 billion, raising the low end of the range.

For the fourth quarter, Meta guided revenue of $73 billion to $76 billion. The midpoint of that range sits above consensus of about $73.6 billion.

The company also announced the establishment of a new non-voting Class C common stock, without further detail in its headline results. Attention is likely to turn to how Meta plans to use the new share class, and to whether the operating miss reflects mainly the one-off legal cost or a broader rise in spending as the company presses ahead with its artificial intelligence investment. I suspect proceeds from sales of this class of stock will be used to help fund AI spending while not diluting Mr. Zuck's control of the firm.

item.title: New Zealand CPI preview: Q3 inflation seen easing to 3.8% ahead of likely RBNZ hike
item.description:
NZD/USD heads into the release around 0.57, having recovered part of its slide to a mid-October low, its weakest level since April 2025. A headline print at or above 3.9%, or firmer core readings, would likely lock in hike pricing and support the kiwi. A result near 3.7% could trim those odds at the margin without derailing them. Beyond today’s number, oil remains the dominant driver: with crude elevated and the currency weaker, imported energy costs are set to keep New Zealand’s inflation outlook, and the RBNZ’s tightening bias, tilted to the upside into year-end.

New Zealand’s Q3 inflation is expected to ease only briefly, with oil and a softer currency already lining up a fourth-quarter rebound that keeps the RBNZ on a hiking path.

Summary:

  • Q3 CPI is due from Statistics NZ at 10:45am Wellington time on Thursday
  • Consensus sees annual inflation at 3.8%, down from 4.1%, against the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection; quarterly CPI is seen at 0.8%, down from 1.5%
  • Forecasts range from 3.7% (Westpac) to 4.0%, with ANZ at 3.8% and BNZ at 3.9%
  • Lower average fuel prices drive the Q3 easing, partly offset by council rates, building costs and food
  • Swaps price around an 80% chance of a 25bp hike to 3.00% on October 28
  • Renewed Middle East hostilities and a weaker NZD point to a Q4 rebound, with some forecasts as high as 4.7%

New Zealand’s third-quarter consumer price index, due from Statistics NZ at 10:45am Wellington time on Thursday, is expected to show annual inflation easing to 3.8% from 4.1% in the June quarter, according to the median of 16 economists surveyed by Bloomberg. That would leave inflation well above the Reserve Bank of New Zealand’s 1% to 3% target band, and only marginally below the central bank’s own 3.9% projection from its September Monetary Policy Statement.

On a quarterly basis, prices are forecast to rise 0.8%. That is a sharp slowdown from 1.5% in the second quarter and matches the RBNZ’s projection exactly. The easing largely reflects lower average fuel costs over the quarter, after the Middle East conflict pushed pump prices sharply higher in the June period. Westpac estimates that cheaper petrol and diesel will take around 0.4 percentage points off quarterly inflation.

Forecasts span a relatively wide range. Westpac sits at the low end at 3.7%. It expects a 0.7% quarterly rise as softer fuel prices are offset by higher council rates, building costs and food prices. ANZ forecasts 3.8% and BNZ 3.9%, while other economists see annual inflation holding at 4.0%. Westpac also expects core inflation measures to remain firm, with some closely watched gauges seen rising to the top of the RBNZ’s target band.

The release is the last major data point before the RBNZ’s October 28 decision. The central bank lifted the Official Cash Rate to 2.75% in September, and swaps markets price around an 80% chance of a further quarter-point increase to 3.00%. ING said it expects a 25 basis point hike barring a major downside surprise. It added that even a small upside surprise would reinforce expectations of a move.

Economists broadly view any third-quarter easing as temporary. Renewed hostilities in the Middle East have pushed New Zealand fuel prices back above their April highs. The New Zealand dollar is also trading roughly 4% below the average level the RBNZ assumed for the fourth quarter. Some local forecasts now see annual inflation accelerating to as high as 4.7% in the December quarter, against the RBNZ’s 3.9% projection. RBNZ chief economist Paul Conway has flagged upside risk to the near-term outlook from oil and the currency.

The core inflation detail may matter as much as the headline. ANZ has said the RBNZ will be watching for signs that higher fuel costs are spreading into broader price pressures. That test will shape not only next week’s decision but also the path into December, when the bank is next scheduled to publish fresh forecasts.

This article was written by Eamonn Sheridan at investinglive.com.

item.title: NZDUSD Technicals: The NZDUSD is stretching to a new high since September 23.
item.description:
The NZDUSD is stretching to the upside, reaching its highest level since September 23. Buyers have been rebuilding the technical picture after the pair’s decline from the August 21 high at 0.59868 to last Wednesday’s low at 0.55645.

That recovery has developed one step at a time. First, the price broke above a downward-sloping trendline. Then it moved above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages and started to put some distance between the price and those technical barometers. A subsequent break above the swing area between 0.56256 and 0.56333 gave buyers another reason to push higher.

Today, the pair cleared another swing area between 0.5673 and 0.5686. The encouraging part for buyers was what happened next: the price rotated back toward the top of that area, found support, and turned higher again. That successful retest helped propel the pair to a session high near 0.5704.

The buyers are making a play. But there is another important hurdle ahead.

What comes next?

The next key upside target is the 38.2% retracement of the decline from the August 21 high at 0.57258.

Why does that level matter? After a strong trend move lower, I look at the 38.2% retracement as a minimum benchmark for judging whether buyers are making a more meaningful challenge to that trend.

The recovery has improved the shorter-term bias, but a move above 0.57258—and the ability to stay above it—would strengthen the case that buyers are taking back more control. If the price stalls below that retracement, the broader move can still be viewed as a correction within the preceding downtrend.

The distinction matters. A rally gives buyers an opportunity. Getting above key resistance and staying above it provides stronger technical confirmation.

Where is the risk for buyers?

On the downside, the low of the broken swing area near 0.56736 is now an important support level. Buyers would want to see that level hold to keep the breakout intact.

For now, the progression favors the buyers: break resistance, hold it on a retest, and extend toward the next target. Their job is to keep that sequence going.

item.title: Bitcoin shows some buying life as risk-on flows return and push the digital currency higher

  • Indirects: 58.2% vs the average of 65.2%

  • Dealers: 10.3% vs the average of 11.9%

Auction grade: C

A mixed auction overall. The Treasury had to pay 0.9 basis points above the WI yield to get the bonds sold, a larger concession than the average of 0.2 basis points. Indirect demand was also softer than average. On the positive side, bid to cover was stronger, direct bidders stepped up, and dealers were left with less supply than usual. Those demand measures help offset the weaker pricing, but the larger tail keeps this from earning an above-average grade.

Generally speaking, the 20 year issue is not a strong part of the yield curve. With the 20 year yield higher than the 30 year yield at 5.4133%, and also higher than the 10 year yield of 5.106%,suggests less overall demand by investors. In a normal positive slope yield curve which we have, the yield should be lower than the 30 year but higher than the 10 year.

item.title: European stocks close higher, but French yields hit their highest since 2002
item.description:
As London and European traders head home, the major European stock indices are closing higher. Germany’s DAX led the advance, while the UK’s FTSE 100 lagged but still finished with a modest gain.

  • German DAX: +342.67 points or 1.35% at 25,647.10

  • France CAC: +83.19 points or 1.06% at 7,921.69

  • Spain IBEX: +231.10 points or 1.21% at 19,323.50

  • Italy FTSE MIB: +572.32 points or 1.17% at 49,643.68

One headline getting attention came from a US official who said Russia accepted the American proposal for a trilateral meeting with Ukraine. Subsequent reporting says the Kremlin agreed to renewed technical-level talks on or after November 10, potentially in Abu Dhabi. That is a step forward, although agreeing to meet leaves the difficult negotiations ahead.

For traders, the importance stretches beyond the diplomatic headlines. Russia matters for oil, refined products, and natural gas. My view is that credible progress toward peace could give Trump more political room to work with Putin on energy and economic issues. But that room depends on results. A meeting alone will not remove the political backlash or resolve the uncertainty around supplies and sanctions.

The markets need peace to make that story more durable. Progress could ease some of the geopolitical premium in energy prices and improve confidence around future supply. Another disappointment would leave traders vulnerable to the next headline and the next shove. Oil and European natural gas remain markets to watch closely as the diplomatic process develops.

Zelenskyy has also been working the diplomatic channels. In Oslo on Tuesday, he met Norwegian Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre, Finnish President Alexander Stubb, and US envoy Steve Witkoff, with Jared Kushner joining remotely. The discussions covered security guarantees, sanctions, reconstruction, air defense, and a possible meeting between the leaders. Zelenskyy also confirmed that US early-warning intelligence for Russian missile attacks was working again. Ukraine’s position included support for a mutual halt to attacks on energy infrastructure.

That puts the focus on what follows the meetings. The diplomatic activity gives traders something to work with, but concrete commitments—and whether the parties follow through—will determine whether the optimism lasts.

France, meanwhile, remains a problem in the bond market. Its benchmark 10-year yield pushed above 5%, reaching its highest level since 2002, as investors continued to question the country’s fiscal position. Higher borrowing costs add to the challenge of bringing its finances under control.

In the supplied afternoon snapshot, France’s 10-year yield was 5.009%, up 6.4 basis points. Germany’s equivalent yield was only 0.4 basis point higher at 3.421%, leaving the French premium at roughly 159 basis points. That divergence is the warning. French stocks participated in today’s rally, but the bond market continues to demand more compensation for holding French debt.

The 100-day moving average has attracted sellers, but the rejection alone does not establish a lasting high. Sellers need follow-through below the nearby retracement and swing levels. Without that progress, this could still be a correction within the rebound from last week’s low.

In the video above, I take a look at the AUDUSD’s rejection at the 100-day moving average, the levels sellers need to break to gain more control, and what would put buyers back in charge.

item.title: US stocks open higher as earnings and AI demand take center stage
item.description:
US stocks are opening higher, giving buyers the early advantage as investors digest earnings from SpaceX and Netflix, a stronger outlook from Super Micro Computer, and fresh AI announcements from Nvidia.

  • Dow Industrial Average: The Dow is modestly higher to kickstart the day

  • S&P 500: The broader S&P is up 18 points or 0.24%

  • Nasdaq Composite: The tech heavy Nasdaq composite index is leading with a gain of 140 points or 0.56%

SpaceX climbs as AI and Starlink drive growth

SpaceX shares are trading higher by around 8.6% following a strong third-quarter report. Revenue surged 161% from a year ago to $14.6 billion, while net income reached $4.4 billion, reversing a year-earlier loss of $1.1 billion. Its Super Intelligence segment generated $7.6 billion in revenue, while Starlink finished the quarter with 13.6 million consumer subscribers, an increase of 1.6 million from the previous quarter. The growth is substantial, but so is the investment: quarterly capital spending totaled approximately $19.6 billion.

The price of SpaceX shares are back above the 200 and 100 hour MAs at $153.81 and 157.51 respectively. The low today held the 100 hour MA with a low at $158.20. Staying above is bullish and keeps the buyers in control. 

Netflix falls as guidance overshadows an earnings beat

Netflix is seeing the opposite reaction, with shares down 4.5%. Third-quarter earnings of $0.87 per share beat expectations of $0.82, while revenue increased 11.8% to $12.87 billion. However, fourth-quarter guidance disappointed, with projected earnings of $0.67 per share below expectations of $0.73 and revenue of approximately $13.44 billion also below forecasts. Netflix additionally reduced its full-year advertising revenue outlook to approximately $2.7 billion from $3 billion, citing a slower rollout of some advertising capabilities.

The reaction provides a useful reminder for traders: an earnings beat does not guarantee a higher stock price. Investors also weigh what comes next against what was already expected. For Netflix, concerns about the outlook are carrying more weight than the latest quarter’s earnings beat.

Netflix shares are trading at the lowest level since August 2024 with a low today aof $64.10.  The high price reached in July 2025 reached $134.12.  

SMCI raises its outlook on stronger AI demand

Super Micro Computer is adding to the positive AI backdrop after sharply raising its preliminary revenue estimate for the September quarter. The company now expects fiscal first-quarter revenue of $18.5 billion to $19.5 billion, up from previous guidance of $14.5 billion to $15.5 billion, primarily reflecting stronger demand for AI platforms. At the midpoint, that is a $4 billion increase, or nearly 27%.

The improvement also extends to profitability. SMCI now expects gross margins of 12% to 12.5%, compared with its previous range of 10.4% to 10.8%, primarily because of its customer and product mix. Higher revenue alongside better margins gives investors two positives to consider ahead of the full quarterly results on November 3.

SMCI’s update provides evidence that demand for AI systems is running ahead of its earlier expectations. That brings Nvidia into focus as well. The servers need computing power, and Nvidia’s latest announcements highlight how the company is expanding its reach across the infrastructure supporting that demand. Shares are trading up near 14% in early trading.

Nvidia expands its AI partnerships

CEO Jensen Huang announced a series of partnerships during his keynote address and said Nvidia has invested nearly $10 billion across Europe over the past year, including investments in 14 European startups in the past week.

Among the announcements, Google Cloud plans to scale Nvidia’s Vera Rubin infrastructure to 960,000 GPUs. Partnerships with Schneider Electric and Infineon focus on the data centers and power systems needed to support that expansion, while work with Nokia aims to bring more AI capabilities into telecommunications networks.

The announcements extend beyond the chips themselves. Nvidia is also expanding its work with Dell, HPE and CrowdStrike across enterprise AI and security. For the broader stock market, that highlights how AI spending reaches across suppliers, infrastructure providers and business applications. Investors will continue to judge how effectively those investments translate into revenue and earnings.

For Nvidia traders, that provides the fundamental backdrop. Now the price action needs to confirm the story. Today’s gains give buyers their opportunity, but getting above resistance—and staying above it—is what would strengthen the technical case.

Looking at the hourly chart, Nvidia has tested its 100-day moving average, currently at $214.62, several times since last Wednesday. The price dipped below that key longer-term barometer on Wednesday, Friday and again yesterday. Each time, however, sellers failed to build downside momentum.

The sellers had their shot. They could not get the price to break and run.

Today, buyers are pushing back. Nvidia has traded as high as $222.16 and is currently near $221, up about $4.50 on the day. That moves the price away from the 100-day moving average and gives buyers some breathing room. However, holding support is only the first step. There is still work to do before buyers can claim more control.

The next hurdle comes near $225, where the 200-hour moving average and a broken upward-sloping trendline converge. Getting back above that area would be a positive step. Above that, the 100-hour moving average at $227.55 becomes the next target.

Those levels provide a roadmap. Move above $225 and then $227.55—and stay above them—and the technical picture improves. Buyers would have reclaimed both hourly moving averages and moved back above the broken trendline, opening the door for a potential run toward the all-time high at $243.37.

Until then, this remains a rebound from important support with resistance still overhead. If sellers stall the recovery at those hurdles, they keep the opportunity to push back toward the 100-day moving average.

The lesson for traders is straightforward: a successful defense of support gives buyers a chance. Reclaiming resistance helps confirm they are taking control. Nvidia has accomplished the first part. Now buyers need to follow through.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.
